entries.title: Breakfast at Brennan's
entries.say: As it reads: Breakfast at Brennan's.
entries.summary: Breakfast at Brennan's is the house's defining idea: a long, celebratory morning meal of an eye opener, a soup, an egg dish and a flamed dessert. Learn its shape, the plates on their foundations and how to sell the morning.
entries.guest: Breakfast here is a celebration rather than a quick bite: a morning cocktail, a soup, one of our egg dishes and Bananas Foster flamed at your table. The Traditional Breakfast brings you all of it.

paras: Breakfast at Brennan's is not a dish but a shape: a long, celebratory morning meal taken in courses, the way most restaurants serve dinner. It is the idea the house is known for, and still the reason many guests come to 417 Royal Street. A server who understands the shape can guide any table, whether the guest wants one plate or the whole ritual.

The shape has four parts: an eye opener, which is a morning cocktail; a soup; an egg dish; and a dessert flamed at the table. Everything else on the breakfast menu, the sweet starters, the omelette, the waffle and the sides, fits around those four.

Owen Brennan noticed that most New Orleans restaurants served only lunch and dinner. He took his cue from Dinner at Antoine's, Frances Parkinson Keyes's popular 1948 novel, and asked why not Breakfast at Brennan's. He made the morning an occasion: something to wake the palate, something warm, the egg dishes the house became known for, and a flame to finish. His story, and his sister Ella's, has its own entry.
The idea outlived him. Bananas Foster, created at Brennan's in 1951, became the flame that ends the meal. Breakfast and lunch now runs from 9 to 2 on weekdays and from 8 to 2 at weekends.

The Traditional Breakfast at Brennan's walks a guest through the whole ritual, with tasting portions of each course and every listed drink in the one price. It opens with the eye opener, a Brandy Milk Punch of brandy, cream, vanilla and nutmeg. A baked apple with an oat and pecan crumble follows, then turtle soup or seafood gumbo with a Bloody Bull, a Bloody Mary made with beef bouillon.

Next come the Eggs Hussarde with 120 ml (4 oz) of Champagne, a petite filet mignon with 120 ml (4 oz) of Côtes du Rhône, and Bananas Foster flamed at the table with chicory coffee. That is roughly four drinks in a morning, so offer a spirit-free drink in place of any pour without being asked; the price does not change. Read the printed card on shift, since courses and pours can change.

The other plates stand on classical foundations. The Framboise French Toast is pain perdu, lost bread: housemade citrus brioche soaked in custard and fried, classically in butter. The Crab & Corn Omelette starts from the omelette, eggs cooked fast in a buttered pan; whether it is rolled the French way or folded is a question for lineup, the short staff meeting before each service. The Duck Confit Waffle carries a Rohan duck leg cooked slowly in fat, which is confit, then crisped. The Café Brûlot Coffee Cake borrows the flavours of the flaming spiced coffee without the flame.

The sides round out an egg dish: Brabant potatoes (bra-BAHNT), cubes fried crisp and, in the old Creole way, tossed in butter, garlic and parsley, with the house finish confirmed at lineup; creamed spinach, squeezed dry and bound with cream; Cheddar Grits; and an Egg Any Style. Children ten and under have their own breakfast at one set price covering fruit, the plate, ice cream and a drink: eggs any style with toast and bacon, vanilla French toast with berries, popcorn shrimp or a grilled cheese, the last two with Brabant potatoes.

Sell the morning as a sequence, not a single plate. A first-time table hears the classic in one breath: a Brandy Milk Punch, the turtle soup, the Eggs Hussarde and Bananas Foster at the table, with the Traditional Breakfast as the easy yes if they want all of it. Seed the Foster as the main courses are ordered, since it is made for two or more. Then pace it: drinks first, soup while the kitchen cooks the eggs, the cart once plates are cleared.

Write every egg style exactly as the guest says it. Questions about what is in a dish, an allergy or a diet go to the kitchen every time: the breakfast is built on eggs, butter and cream, so never guess at a plate.

faults.fault: The table orders one plate each and nothing more
faults.cause: The server sold a dish rather than the morning.
faults.fix: Name the four parts and offer the Traditional Breakfast as the whole story in one order.

faults.fault: Eggs come back to the kitchen
faults.cause: The style was not asked, or not written exactly.
faults.fix: Ask the style and write it word for word, from the styles confirmed at lineup: sunny side up, over easy, over medium, over hard, scrambled or soft-boiled.

faults.fault: No Bananas Foster at the end
faults.cause: It was mentioned too late, when the table was already full.
faults.fix: Seed it with the main course order; it is made at the table for two or more.

faults.fault: A guest has had too much to drink before noon
faults.cause: The tasting's four pours add up in a morning.
faults.fix: Offer a spirit-free drink in place of any pour, unasked; the tasting price does not change.

brennans.how: The Framboise French Toast is pain perdu made with housemade citrus brioche, mascarpone mousse, raspberry coulis and local raspberries; it sits among the starters, so offer it for the table to share before the egg dishes.

The Crab & Corn Omelette is filled with Louisiana lump crab and roasted sweet corn, with miso butter, lemon, basil and a Marcona almond gremolata; ask at lineup whether it is rolled French style or folded.

The Rohan duck leg is confit, cooked slowly in fat and crisped, on a cornbread and chive waffle with foie gras butter, mustard maple syrup and a sunny-side-up egg. Describe the method, and promise no house times.

The coffee cake borrows the flaming coffee's flavours: chicory coffee and bittersweet chocolate cake, pecans, a spiced citrus glaze and whipped crème fraîche. The drink itself is not on our list, so sell the flavours, not the flame.
Brabant potatoes are a breakfast side: cubed potatoes fried golden and crisp, then tossed in butter with garlic and parsley in the old Creole way. Confirm the house finish and the fryer at lineup.
Creamed spinach is a breakfast and lunch side, spinach squeezed dry and bound with cream; whether it is the same preparation as the Parmesan spinach under the Sardou is a question for the kitchen.
Cheddar Grits are coarse-ground corn simmered slowly until creamy and finished with cheddar; whether they are stone-ground, and whose corn, are questions for the kitchen.
An Egg Any Style is one egg cooked as the guest asks: sunny side up, over easy, medium or hard, scrambled or soft-boiled. Write the style exactly, and confirm the styles offered at lineup.
The children's eggs any style come with toast and bacon; ask the parent how the child likes them and write the style on the ticket word for word.
The children's vanilla French toast is the same lost bread idea in a plainer form, with fresh berries and whipped cream, inside the one set price for children ten and under.
On the children's breakfast the popcorn shrimp come with Brabant potatoes, the crisp cubed potatoes of the old Creole dining rooms.
The children's grilled cheese sandwich is served with Brabant potatoes, so a child gets the same crisp New Orleans side as the grown-ups.

cards.front: What is Breakfast at Brennan's, in one sentence?
cards.back: A long, celebratory morning meal in courses, Owen Brennan's idea, built when most New Orleans restaurants served only lunch and dinner.

cards.front: Which novel gave Owen Brennan his cue for Breakfast at Brennan's?
cards.back: Dinner at Antoine's, Frances Parkinson Keyes's popular 1948 novel; he asked why not Breakfast at Brennan's.

cards.front: What are the four parts of the Brennan's breakfast?
cards.back: An eye opener, a soup, an egg dish and a flamed dessert; the Traditional Breakfast keeps that order, with a baked apple before the soup and a petite filet after the eggs.

cards.front: What is an eye opener, and which one opens the tasting?
cards.back: A morning cocktail to start breakfast; the Traditional Breakfast opens with a Brandy Milk Punch of brandy, cream, vanilla and nutmeg.

cards.front: What does the Traditional Breakfast include?
cards.back: Tasting portions and every listed drink: milk punch, baked apple, soup with a Bloody Bull, Eggs Hussarde with Champagne, petite filet with red, Foster with chicory coffee.

cards.front: What foundation stands under the Framboise French Toast?
cards.back: Pain perdu, lost bread: stale bread soaked in egg and milk and fried in butter, here made with housemade citrus brioche.

cards.front: What does confit mean on the Duck Confit Waffle?
cards.back: The Rohan duck leg is cooked slowly, submerged in fat, until tender, then crisped skin side down before it goes on the waffle.

cards.front: How does the Café Brûlot Coffee Cake relate to café brûlot?
cards.back: It borrows the flaming coffee's flavours, chicory coffee, chocolate and spiced citrus, without the flame; the drink itself is not on our list.

cards.front: What are Brabant potatoes?
cards.back: A New Orleans side: potatoes cut into cubes, fried crisp and tossed in butter, garlic and parsley. Confirm the house finish at lineup.

cards.front: What does the children's breakfast price cover?
cards.back: For guests ten and under, one set price covers fruit, the plate, ice cream and a drink, so tell the parents the whole price at once.

cards.front: How do you sell breakfast at Brennan's?
cards.back: As a sequence, not a single plate: something to start, an egg dish and the Foster to finish, with the tasting as the easy yes.

cards.front: Why offer a spirit-free drink during the Traditional Breakfast?
cards.back: Its pours add up to roughly four drinks in a morning, so offer a spirit-free swap for any pour, unasked, with no change in price.

Café brûlot
Brennan's Irish Coffee

Full portions and a bottle of Champagne
The egg course and coffee, with dessert extra

questions.q: Which classical foundation stands under the Framboise French Toast?
questions.answer: Pain perdu

Pâte à choux
Crêpes Suzette
questions.why: Pain perdu, lost bread, rescues bread by soaking it in egg and milk and frying it in butter; here the bread is housemade citrus brioche.

entries.title: Flambé and tableside service
entries.summary: Tableside service brings the last of the cooking into the dining room, on a cart called a guéridon. Learn where it comes from, the flamed desserts it carries at Brennan's, the choreography at the cart and why New Orleans kept it.
entries.guest: Dessert here can be finished right beside your table: Bananas Foster is cooked on the cart, flamed with rum and spooned over our vanilla ice cream.

paras: Tableside service is cooking, carving or finishing a dish in the dining room, in front of the guest. It is done on a guéridon (gay-ree-DOHN), a small wheeled table or cart that carries a burner, a pan and everything the dish needs. Flambé (flahm-BAY) means flamed: spirit added to a hot pan and lit, so the alcohol vapour burns above the sauce in a short burst of flame.

It matters because it is the moment many guests remember from Brennan's, and because it turns a server into a cook in full view. Done well, it is theatre and flavour at once; done carelessly, it is a fire in a full room.

The guéridon belongs to the grand dining rooms of Europe, where a maître d'hôtel, the head waiter, or a captain, the senior server who runs a section, carved, dressed and flamed beside the table. American hotel schools call this French service, although in France the old service à la française meant every dish of a course set on the table at once. That gave way in the nineteenth century to service à la russe, courses brought in order, and the cart became the stage for the last touch.

Cherries Jubilee is the old flamed classic. It is generally credited to Auguste Escoffier for one of Queen Victoria's jubilees, most often said to be the Diamond Jubilee of 1897, though some accounts give the Golden Jubilee of 1887. His version was poached cherries in a thickened syrup with warmed kirsch, a cherry brandy, lit at the table, and no ice cream; the ice cream came later, largely in America.

Across most of America, tableside cooking faded in the later twentieth century as plates came to be finished in the kitchen. One reason often given for its survival here is that the old New Orleans houses kept career waiters and captains, rooms built for occasion and dishes whose whole point is the flame, and visitors came looking for exactly that.

Cherries Jubilee is the eldest of a small family. Crêpes Suzette, thin pancakes flamed in an orange butter sauce, come from the same European rooms. Café brûlot is the New Orleans cousin: brandy and orange liqueur flamed with spices and citrus peel, then ladled into strong coffee, a ritual Antoine's credits to Jules Alciatore. Bananas Foster is the Brennan's signature. Each has its own entry.

The choreography is learned before the first flame. The cart is set first: burner checked, pan, the spirit already measured into a small vessel, a lid, the plates, and ice cream timed to arrive cold. It stands where nothing hangs overhead, away from drapes and air vents, with menus and napkins cleared, and the guests stay seated and back from it. In many rooms one person cooks and flames while a second serves, so the dessert lands while the ice cream still holds its shape; at Brennan's, who does what is a question for the manager.

The spirit goes in only with the pan pulled off the flame, never from the bottle and never into a pan already alight; the far edge is tilted to the burner so the flame rises away from cook and guests. Let it burn out before plating, and turn the burner off before leaving the cart. Flaming burns the vapour, not all the alcohol; much stays in the sauce. Flambé safety in full has its own entry.

Bananas Foster is the house signature: bananas in a blond, bubbling caramel of butter, brown sugar and cinnamon, flamed with rum and spooned over housemade vanilla ice cream, made in one pan for two or more. Cherries Jubilee, fresh tart black cherries in a Luxardo sauce flamed over the same ice cream, is not on the dessert menu of 3 October 2026, so confirm with a manager before offering it. Who performs the flambé, and the sign-off before a new server lights a pan, are questions for training.

Read the room before the cart rolls: an anniversary table wants a hushed show, a birthday table the whole story. Tell the story before the flame, while the caramel bubbles: 1951, named for Richard Foster, in the house's telling once a manager has confirmed it. Then go quiet: the pan needs your full attention, and the flame is the line. In a bright morning room the flame can be almost invisible, so treat the pan as lit until it has clearly died down.

faults.cause: The caramel was too cool, or the rum had no time to warm and give off vapour.
faults.fix: Bring the caramel to a full bubble first and let the rum warm in the pan for a few seconds before tilting it to the flame; never add more spirit to a pan that may already be alight.

faults.cause: Too much spirit, or spirit poured from the bottle.
faults.fix: Measure into a small vessel beforehand and keep a lid within reach to smother the pan.

faults.fault: A flame that reaches something overhead
faults.cause: The cart was set under a vent, drape or low décor.
faults.fix: Set the cart where nothing hangs overhead, away from drapes and air vents, before the burner is lit.

faults.fault: A guest too close to the pan
faults.cause: Guests leaning in, or a child, loose sleeve or long hair near the cart.
faults.fix: Seat everyone back from the cart before the spirit goes in.

faults.fault: The ice cream melts before it reaches the guest
faults.cause: Scooped too early, or one person cooking and serving alone.
faults.fix: Time the ice cream to the flame, with a second pair of hands if the house works that way.

brennans.how: Bananas Foster is made on the guéridon: butter, brown sugar and cinnamon taken to a blond caramel, bananas turned once, rum added off the flame and lit, then spooned over vanilla ice cream, for two or more.

Fresh tart black cherries in a Luxardo sauce are flamed at the table over housemade vanilla ice cream. It is off the 3 October 2026 dessert menu, so confirm with a manager; ask the chef which spirit is lit and whether the cherries are pitted.

cards.front: What is a guéridon in the dining room?
cards.back: A small wheeled table or cart beside the guest, with a burner and a pan, on which a dish is carved, finished or flamed.

cards.front: What does flambé mean, and what actually burns?
cards.back: Flamed: spirit added to a hot pan and lit. Only the alcohol vapour burns, so a cool pan will not catch, and much of the alcohol stays in the sauce.

cards.front: What do American hotel schools call guéridon service, and what did the term once mean in France?
cards.back: French service; in France the old service à la française meant every dish of a course set on the table at once.

cards.front: Who is credited with Cherries Jubilee, and for what occasion?
cards.back: Auguste Escoffier, for one of Queen Victoria's jubilees, most often said to be 1897; his version used warmed kirsch and no ice cream.

cards.front: What is the Brennan's Cherries Jubilee, and what must you check first?
cards.back: Fresh tart black cherries in a Luxardo sauce flamed over vanilla ice cream; it is off the current dessert menu, so confirm with a manager, and ask the kitchen whether the cherries are pitted.

cards.front: What was service à la russe?
cards.back: Courses brought in order, one after another; it replaced service à la française in the nineteenth century and left the cart for the last touch.

cards.front: What is café brûlot, the New Orleans cousin of the flamed desserts?
cards.back: Brandy and orange liqueur flamed with spices and citrus peel, then ladled into strong coffee; Antoine's credits Jules Alciatore with it.

cards.front: Why do many rooms have one person flame and another serve?
cards.back: So the dessert lands while the ice cream is still cold and the cook's eyes never leave the pan; at Brennan's the manager says who does what.

cards.front: When does the spirit go into the pan?
cards.back: Measured beforehand into a small vessel, and added only with the pan pulled off the flame: never from the bottle, never into a lit pan.

cards.front: How do you read the room and time your words at the cart?
cards.back: Read the room first: a hushed show for an anniversary, the whole story for a birthday. Tell the story before the flame, while the caramel bubbles; go quiet as the rum goes in, eyes on the pan, guests seated and back.

cards.front: Why did tableside cooking last in New Orleans?
cards.back: The reasons often given: the old houses kept career waiters and captains, rooms built for occasion and dishes whose point is the flame, and visitors came for exactly that.

cards.front: Why treat the pan as lit in a bright breakfast room?
cards.back: Daylight can make the flame almost invisible, so the pan stays dangerous until the flame has clearly died down.

questions.q: In tableside service, what is a guéridon?
questions.answer: A wheeled cart with a burner beside the table
distractors: A copper pan for caramel
A long-handled lighter for igniting the spirit
The captain's station by the door
questions.why: The guéridon is the cart that carries the burner, the pan and everything prepared for the dish, so the last of the cooking happens in view of the guest.

questions.q: The rum goes into a pan of cool caramel and will not catch. Why?
questions.answer: Too little alcohol vapour rises to burn
distractors: The sugar has not yet caramelised
The butter in the caramel smothers the flame
Rum burns only in a copper pan
questions.why: Only the alcohol vapour burns, and a cool pan gives off too little of it: bring the caramel to a full bubble and let the rum warm a few seconds, never adding more spirit.

questions.q: Escoffier's Cherries Jubilee: which spirit was lit, and was it served with ice cream?
questions.answer: Warmed kirsch, and no ice cream
distractors: Dark rum, over vanilla ice cream
Cognac, with whipped cream
Grand Marnier, over crêpes
questions.why: His version was poached cherries in a thickened syrup lit with warm kirsch; the ice cream is a later, largely American habit.

questions.q: A guest asks for Cherries Jubilee. What do you do first?
questions.answer: Confirm with a manager that it is served
distractors: Fire it straight away with the Foster
Tell the guest it was retired years ago
Offer to flame it with a spirit of their choice
questions.why: It is not on the dessert menu of 3 October 2026, so a manager confirms it before it is offered or promised.

questions.q: Which service style brought courses to the table one after another?
questions.answer: Service à la russe
distractors: Service à la française
Family-style service
Buffet service
questions.why: Service à la russe brought courses in order and replaced service à la française, where every dish of a course was set out at once; the cart kept the last touch.

questions.q: When is the rum added to the Bananas Foster pan?
questions.answer: Off the flame, from a measured vessel
distractors: Straight from the bottle over the burner
Into the pan once it is already alight
Before the butter and sugar go in
questions.why: Measured spirit, added with the pan pulled away from the flame, keeps the bottle and the cook's hand away from a burst of fire.

questions.q: An anniversary couple at a quiet corner table orders the Foster. How does reading the room shape the service?
questions.answer: A hushed show, the story kept short
distractors: The full story, told for the whole room
No flame, plated in the kitchen instead
The next table invited over to watch
questions.why: Reading the room comes before the cart rolls: an anniversary wants a hushed show, a birthday the whole story. Either way the story comes before the flame, and quiet during it.

questions.q: Tableside cooking faded across most of America. Which reason is often given for its survival in the old New Orleans dining rooms?
questions.answer: They kept career waiters and captains
distractors: A city ordinance required flamed desserts
Rum was cheaper at the port
Their kitchens were too small for desserts
questions.why: The reasons often given: the old houses kept career waiters and captains, rooms built for occasion and dishes whose point is the flame, and visitors came looking for exactly that.

questions.q: Which flamed New Orleans ritual is the coffee cousin of Bananas Foster?
questions.answer: Café brûlot
distractors: Café au lait
Irish coffee
Café glacé
questions.why: Café brûlot flames brandy and orange liqueur with spices and citrus peel, then ladles it into strong coffee at the table.

entries.title: The menu read by method
entries.say: As it reads: the menu read by method.
entries.summary: The Brennan's menu read by method rather than by dish: steam in a leaf, a blackening pan, the fryer, slow fat, the roasting pan, the rice pot, and the pastry kitchen's custards, caramel and laminated dough. A map from technique to plate.
entries.guest: Our kitchen cooks each plate its own way: the Gulf fish steams in a banana leaf, the poussin is brined in sweet tea and fried, and the tasting's duck breast is roasted crisp.

paras: A menu read by method is a menu you can explain without memorising it. Every plate is a technique applied to an ingredient, and the technique tells you the texture, the timing and the honest words for the guest.

Ask four questions of any plate. What is the cooking medium: steam, dry heat, hot fat, or none at all? How hot, and for how long? What does that do to texture: moist, crusted, crisp or silky? And what does it mean for the ticket: a cooking time, a doneness to ask, a raw food advisory?

Steam and fierce heat. The Gulf Fish en Papillote is the classical parcel in banana leaf instead of paper, sealed and baked, classically in a hot oven around 205°C (400°F) for 10 to 15 minutes, so the fish steams in its own juices, here with crab, sorghum, olives, tomato and Marcona almonds. The Blackened Tofu takes Paul Prudhomme's method from K-Paul's, around 1980, onto local tofu: a spice crust charred dark in a minute or two a side in a dry cast-iron pan heated past smoking. Prudhomme dipped his fish in butter first, so ask the kitchen before anyone says vegan.

Fat, fast and slow. The Poussin à la Moutarde is a Cornish hen soaked in a sweet tea brine of strong black tea, sugar and salt, coated and fried until the skin is crisp and the thickest part of the thigh reads 74°C (165°F), then sauced with a Burgundian mustard cream, the mustard stirred in off the heat so it keeps its bite; how long it brines and how it is fried are chef questions. The Rohan (ROH-han) duck leg is confit, cooked slowly under fat and crisped for the Duck Confit Waffle: describe the method, and promise no house times.

The roasting pan and the spice shelf. The Rohan breast is scored and started skin down in a cold or moderate pan so its fat renders slowly and the skin crisps, then finished in the oven, rested and sliced pink, with cane syrup-glazed peaches. The Creole Hanger Steak carries the housemade Creole spice, a pepita persillade of parsley, garlic and toasted pumpkin seeds, and Madeira-glazed broccolini. South Louisiana Rice Dressing folds rice into seasoned minced meat browned with the trinity, often bound with a little roux or gravy, cousin to dirty rice.

The pastry kitchen. The New Orleans Bread Pudding is bread baked in custard, under a whiskey caramel. The Snickers is a milk chocolate Bavarian cream, crème anglaise usually set with gelatine and lightened with whipped cream, with a caramel custard; for a guest who avoids gelatine, the kitchen confirms. The Lemon Tart wears a cooked meringue, Italian or Swiss, toasted with a torch. The Pineapple Tarte Tatin is the upside-down tart: classically the fruit is caramelised in butter and sugar in the pan, covered with puff pastry, baked and turned out so the pastry sits beneath. The puff pastry is laminated, raised by steam from its butter; the sweetened condensed anglaise is a pouring custard, never boiled.

Smaller touches carry methods too: steak tartare, seasoned raw beef, in the fried potato cannoli; brown butter in the financiers of the Blackberry Trifle; the raw Creole tomatoes of the tostada, where the method is restraint; and the children's Gulf fish, simply sautéed and turned once.

Each method has a fault you can learn to see. A papillote left too long dries the fish inside a scorched leaf. A blackening pan held too long turns the crust acrid. Oil that is too cool gives pale, greasy skin. A duck breast started too hot keeps a band of unrendered fat. An anglaise pulled at about 82°C (180°F), when it coats the spoon, is right; taken much past 85°C (185°F) it curdles.

Lead with the method, then the flavour: baked in a banana leaf so it steams in its own juices; brined in sweet tea, fried and sauced with a French mustard cream. Methods also set the clock and the ticket. The parcel and the bone-in bird take far longer than a fillet, so both are fired ahead of the course; the kitchen's fire times are learned at lineup. The duck breast and the hanger need a doneness, and a pink duck breast sits below the Food Code's 74°C (165°F) for poultry, so like the tartare's raw beef it needs a consumer advisory; confirm the house wording at lineup. Allergy questions go to the kitchen.

ratios.label: The holy trinity
ratios.value: Onion, celery and green pepper, often 2 parts onion to 1 each of celery and pepper

ratios.label: Crème anglaise, a classic proportion
ratios.value: 1 litre (about 1 quart) of milk to 8 to 10 yolks and 200 to 250 g (7 to 9 oz) of sugar

ratios.label: Brine for a small bird, a working guide
ratios.value: About 50 g (1 3/4 oz) of salt per 1 litre (about 1 quart) of sweet tea, a few hours; the house time is a question for the chef

ratios.label: Confit cure
ratios.value: Legs salted with garlic and herbs for 12 to 24 hours, rinsed, then 2.5 to 3 hours under fat at a bare tremble, about 90°C (194°F), until the meat yields at the bone and a skewer slides in freely

ratios.label: Bavarian cream
ratios.value: About 15 g (1/2 oz) of gelatine per 1 litre (about 1 quart) of anglaise, with about an equal volume of whipped cream

temps.label: A hot oven for a fish parcel, typically
Frying oil, a common working heat
Duck fat for confit, a bare tremble
Crème anglaise coats the spoon; never boil it
Poultry cooked to, thickest part (FDA Food Code)
Duck breast pulled for medium rare; the house standard is confirmed at lineup

faults.fault: Dry fish in a scorched leaf
faults.cause: The papillote was left in too long or the oven ran too hot.
faults.fix: Time the parcel to the thickness of the fillet and pull it while the fish just flakes.

faults.cause: The spice sat too long in a pan heated past smoking.
faults.fix: About 2 minutes a side over the highest heat, under a strong extractor, until the underside looks charred; the crust should be dark, never burnt.

faults.cause: Oil too cool, or the basket overloaded.
faults.fix: Heat the oil to about 175 to 180°C (347 to 356°F) before loading, fry in small batches, keep it near 160 to 165°C (320 to 329°F) for bone-in pieces and drain on a rack.

faults.fault: Flabby duck skin over a band of fat
faults.cause: The breast went into a pan too hot, so the fat never rendered.
faults.fix: Score it, start it skin down in a cold or moderate pan and render slowly before the turn.

faults.cause: It was boiled, and the yolks set into curds.
faults.fix: Stir gently to about 82°C (180°F), when it coats a spoon, and strain at once into a cold bowl.

brennans.how: The Gulf fish is wrapped in banana leaf rather than paper, with crab, sorghum, olives, tomato and Marcona almonds, so it steams in its own juices; ask at lineup whether it is opened at the table, and warn of the steam.

Prudhomme's blackening, a spice crust toasted dark in a very hot dry pan, is applied to New Orleans Tien Dat tofu; the classic method uses butter, so check with the kitchen before calling the dish vegan.

A Cornish hen brined in sweet tea, fried crisp and sauced with a Burgundian mustard cream, with turnips and shallots: Southern fried chicken under a French bistro sauce, which is the line to give the guest.

On the dinner tasting the Rohan breast is roasted with its fat rendered and its skin crisp, served pink, with cane syrup-glazed peaches and candied hazelnuts; confirm the kitchen's doneness at lineup.
The Rohan duck leg on the breakfast Duck Confit Waffle is confit, cooked slowly in fat and then crisped; describe the method in general and promise no house times.

The Creekstone Farms hanger takes the housemade Creole spice, a pepita persillade of parsley, garlic and toasted pumpkin seed, and Madeira-glazed broccolini; the glaze is made with wine, worth saying to guests who avoid alcohol.
Rice folded into seasoned minced meat browned with the trinity, a dinner side with no description printed; it is cousin to dirty rice, so confirm the meats with the kitchen before describing it.
Bread pudding baked in custard and served with a whiskey caramel, buttermilk ice cream and pralines; the caramel carries whiskey, so tell guests who avoid alcohol.

The chocolate bar rebuilt: a milk chocolate Bavarian cream for the chocolate and a caramel custard for the caramel, with nougat ice cream and roasted peanuts; the house guide flags peanuts, so confirm with the kitchen for every table.
Toasted meringue sits with yuzu mousse, lemon jelly and a sweet pastry crumb, the French lemon tart taken apart; which meringue style the pastry kitchen uses is a question for the chef.

The upside-down tart made with charred pineapple instead of apple, on puff pastry, with a sweetened condensed anglaise and whipped vanilla mousse; whether it is baked inverted or built on the plate is a question for the chef.
Seasoned raw beef is piped into a crisp potato cannoli shell with crème fraîche and grated cured egg yolk; it carries a raw beef advisory, so read the service note and send questions to the kitchen.

The blackberry financier biscuits in the trifle are made with brown butter, which gives them their nutty, buttery taste; financiers are traditionally made with almond flour, so confirm with the kitchen.
Louisiana heirloom and Creole tomatoes are served raw with burrata, an okra tostada and smoked tomato water; the dish follows the season, so expect it to change when the tomatoes finish.
The children's Gulf fish is sautéed: a hot pan, a little fat, left to colour, turned once and finished gently, served with potato and green beans; know today's fish at lineup.

cards.front: What four questions read any plate by method?
cards.back: The cooking medium, the heat and time, what it does to texture, and what it means for the ticket: a time, a doneness or an advisory.

cards.front: How is the Gulf Fish en Papillote cooked?
cards.back: Sealed in a banana leaf rather than paper and baked, so the fish steams in its own juices with crab, olives, tomato and almonds.

cards.front: What is blackening, and who created it?
cards.back: A spice crust toasted dark in a dry cast-iron pan heated past smoking; Paul Prudhomme, at K-Paul's around 1980. Here it is on tofu.

cards.front: Which three methods meet on the Poussin à la Moutarde?
cards.back: A sweet tea brine, the fryer and a Burgundian mustard cream: Southern fried chicken under a French bistro sauce.

cards.front: How is the Rohan duck used twice on the menus?
cards.back: The breast is scored and started skin down in a cold or moderate pan to render its fat, then roasted and served pink on the dinner tasting; the leg is confit on the breakfast waffle.

cards.front: What is the pepita persillade on the Creole Hanger Steak, and what should a guest know about the broccolini?
cards.back: Persillade is parsley and garlic chopped fine and thrown on at the last second; pepitas are hulled pumpkin seeds toasted until they puff. The broccolini's glaze is Madeira reduced until syrupy, so tell guests who avoid alcohol.

cards.front: What is South Louisiana rice dressing?
cards.back: Rice folded into seasoned minced meat browned with the trinity, cousin to dirty rice; confirm the meats with the kitchen, since none are printed.

cards.front: What is the Bavarian cream in The Snickers?
cards.back: A crème anglaise, usually set with gelatine and lightened with whipped cream, here made with milk chocolate, beside a caramel custard. For a guest who avoids gelatine, ask the kitchen.

cards.front: Which foundations meet in the Pineapple Tarte Tatin?
cards.back: Caramel, puff pastry, a laminated dough raised by steam from its butter, and a sweetened condensed anglaise, a pouring custard.

cards.front: Why is a crème anglaise never boiled?
cards.back: Its yolks thicken it at about 82°C (180°F), when it coats a spoon; much hotter and they set into a grainy custard.

cards.front: Name the smaller touches on the menu read by method.
cards.back: Raw steak tartare in the fried potato cannoli, brown butter financiers in the Blackberry Trifle, raw Creole tomatoes on the tostada and the children's sautéed Gulf fish.

cards.front: Which plates set the clock or need a question on the ticket?
cards.back: The papillote and the whole poussin take time; the duck breast and the hanger need a doneness; the pink duck breast and the raw tartare carry an advisory.

questions.q: What wraps the Gulf Fish en Papillote at Brennan's?
questions.answer: A banana leaf
distractors: Parchment paper
Puff pastry
A salt crust
questions.why: The classical papillote is paper; here a banana leaf seals the parcel just as well, so the fish steams in its own juices.

questions.q: Who created the blackening method used on the Blackened Tofu?
questions.answer: Paul Prudhomme
distractors: Auguste Escoffier
Jules Alciatore
Paul Blangé
questions.why: Prudhomme created blackening at K-Paul's around 1980; Alciatore is credited with pompano en papillote and Blangé with Bananas Foster.

questions.q: Which pairing is the whole idea of the Poussin à la Moutarde?
questions.answer: Southern fried chicken under a French bistro sauce
distractors: Roast chicken with a Creole tomato sauce
Grilled quail with a Burgundian red wine reduction
Poached hen with a classic hollandaise
questions.why: A sweet tea-brined, fried Cornish hen meets a Burgundian mustard cream, two traditions on one plate.

questions.q: How is the Rohan duck breast started, so its fat renders and the skin crisps?
questions.answer: Skin down in a cold or moderate pan
distractors: Skin up under a very hot grill
Plunged whole into hot frying oil
Poached in duck fat for hours
questions.why: Skin down in a cold or moderate pan melts the fat slowly as the skin crisps; started too hot, a band of fat stays. The leg, not the breast, is the confit.

questions.q: Before describing the South Louisiana Rice Dressing, what must you confirm?
questions.answer: The meats, with the kitchen
distractors: The rice variety, with the bar
The wine, with the sommelier
Nothing, the menu describes it
questions.why: The menu prints no description, and recipes differ on which meats go in, so the kitchen answers before you describe it.

questions.q: What usually sets a Bavarian cream such as the one in The Snickers?
questions.answer: Gelatine in the custard
distractors: Flour cooked in butter
Egg whites baked until crisp
Cornflour boiled in milk
questions.why: A Bavarian cream is crème anglaise usually set with gelatine and lightened with whipped cream, so it holds its shape yet stays light; ask the kitchen for a guest who avoids gelatine.

questions.q: At roughly what temperature does a crème anglaise coat the spoon?
questions.why: The yolks thicken the custard at about 82°C (180°F); boiling sets them into curds and the anglaise turns grainy.

questions.q: Reading a plate by method, which question belongs on the list?
questions.answer: What is the cooking medium?
distractors: What does it cost to make?
Who on the line cooked it?
Which supplier sent the fish?
questions.why: Medium, heat and time, texture and the ticket are the four questions; the medium, steam, dry heat or fat, comes first.

questions.q: What makes the puff pastry of the Tarte Tatin rise?
questions.answer: Steam from its layered butter
distractors: Yeast proved overnight
Baking powder in the dough
Whisked egg whites folded in
questions.why: Puff pastry is laminated: the water in its butter turns to steam in the oven and pushes the layers apart, with no yeast at all.
